International Journal of Human-Computer Studies

Volume 183, March 2024, 103194

A new dynamic spatial information design framework for AR-HUD to evoke drivers’ instinctive responses and improve accident prevention

Author links open overlay panel, , , ,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhcs.2023.103194Get rights and content
Full text access

Highlights

  • •
    A new framework of AR-HUD design is developed to evoke driver’s instinctive response.
  • •
    The information of the dynamic interface follows the cognitive process of the driver.
  • •
    The interface supports the driver’s cognitive process at three levels of SRK taxonomy.
  • •
    The spatial interface design effectively supports the driver’s situation awareness.

Abstract

Driver’s instinctive responses and skill-based behaviors enable them to react faster and better control their vehicle in dangerous situations. This study incorporated dynamic spatial information design (DSID) in an augmented reality head-up display (AR-HUD) under manual driving conditions. By integrating the skill, rule, and knowledge (SRK) taxonomy and situation awareness (SA) theory, our AR-HUD successfully evoked drivers’ instinctive responses and improved driving safety. First, we converted symbol and sign information processed at the knowledge-based and rule-based levels, respectively, into signal information processed at the skill-based level. Then we developed four AR-HUD interfaces with different dynamic designs for use in a hazardous scenario at an intersection. Finally, we investigated each design’s impact on drivers’ SA and driving performance. Experimental results demonstrated that our DSID enhanced drivers’ SA and accident-avoidance capabilities while reducing their cognitive workload. Among the four AR-HUD interfaces, the one that incorporated all three information elements under study (i.e., lateral warning, dynamic driving space, and speedometer) performed the best. This indicates that our proposed framework has potential applications in other similar dangerous driving scenarios, thus contributing to the development of safer and more efficient driving environments.

Keywords

Skills rules and knowledge (SRK) taxonomy
Augmented reality head-up display (AR-HUD)
Situation awareness (SA)
Dynamic spatial information design (DSID)
Dangerous driving scenarios

1. Introduction

Human driving behavior is based on real-time responses to changes in the environment, which involve various levels of cognitive activities. The skills, rules, and knowledge (SRK) taxonomy theory categorizes human cognitive activities into three levels: skill-based, rule-based, and knowledge-based (Rasmussen, 1987). According to this theory, skill-based behavior is instinctive and automated, and humans have the fastest response time to stimuli at this level. The other two levels require the processing of information based on existing rules or knowledge before taking action, resulting in a slower response time. In fact, a significant cause of accidents is the delayed response or lack of perception of what is in the environment by humans. This suggests that incorporating contextual information that triggers faster instinctive responses can reduce the reaction time of drivers and enable them to make faster decisions to avoid danger.
A good option for triggering quick and appropriate instinctive responses and skill-based behaviors in drivers is projecting virtual information into the real environment. The augmented reality head-up display (AR-HUD) is an advanced interface technology that uses AR to overlay information onto the driver’s real environment. This creates a synchronized space where real and virtual information can appear in real time together (Moussa et al., 2012).
Using AR-HUDs, drivers can maintain their gaze and attention on the road for longer periods, enabling quicker responses to hazards and thereby enhancing driving performance and reducing workload (Kim and Gabbard, 2022). For example, AR information can be superimposed onto other road users to increase the driver’s perception and prediction of pedestrian behavior (Medenica et al., 2011). Additionally, displaying important driving events on the AR-HUD interface can enhance drivers’ situation awareness (SA) (Endsley, 1988, George et al., 2012).
Effective interface design can rapidly direct the driver’s attention to critical elements in the environment related to potential hazards, thereby enhancing the driver’s SA (Endsley, 1988) and improving driving safety. Unfortunately, while overlaying critical information on an AR-HUD windshield display (WSD) can enhance response times (Yoo, 1999, Horrey et al., 2003), poorly designed projections can lead to various issues and human–machine interaction misunderstandings (Ward et al., 1995). Therefore, many studies have focused on designing rational AR-HUD interface messages to best enhance drivers’ SA.
In some studies, SRK taxonomy theory has been used to intervene in the cognitive processes of drivers. For example, Tönnis et al. (2007) designed an AR-HUD interface that displays the estimated braking distance of a vehicle as an AR braking bar on the road ahead. They also mapped the rotation of the steering wheel to the left and right movements of the AR path displayed on the interface. Kim et al. (2013) designed visual information on the AR-HUD that varies according to the distance between the vehicle and the impending danger. In left-turn scenarios, Tran et al. (2013) showed that displaying the projected path of other traffic participants on the AR-HUD can help activate drivers’ instinctive reactions and alleviate visual distraction.
The above-mentioned studies are well-targeted at the driver’s SA, and use the SRK taxonomy to intervene in interface information design, but they do not specifically address interface design for particular types of dangerous situations. Moreover, they only focus on the impacts of the position and dynamic changes in the semantics of interface elements on drivers. In contrast, we investigate the effects of dynamic changes in interface information content (including color, semantics, and morphology) on the SA and driving performance of drivers. Considering that in the future there is a high probability that a vehicle’s whole windshield will be used as an AR-HUD display, all of our AR-HUD interfaces are designed based on the WSD size.
To address the aforementioned gap, the purpose of this study is to explore how to design different levels or types of information in hazardous scenarios to trigger the driver’s instinctive response and driving skills as quickly as possible to avoid danger (using the example of hazardous scenarios at intersections). Therefore, our research questions (RQ) are:
  • •
    RQ1: What SA information in the hazard scenario needs to be shared with the human driver through the interface?
  • •
    RQ2: What method should be used to design dynamic spatial information that meets drivers’ SA needs?
  • •
    RQ3: What are the impacts of different forms of dynamic information design on drivers’ behavior?
To answer RQ1, we reviewed SA theory, conducted cognitive work analysis, and improved use-case diagram construction for the driving task. This process enabled us to identify the information that the Advanced Driving Assist System (ADAS) needs to convey to the driver through the AR-HUD. To address RQ2, we proposed a dynamic spatial information design (DSID) framework based on the SRK taxonomy and SA theory. We then designed cognitive information for the AR-HUD interface in hazardous intersection scenarios and visualized the dynamic information content of the interface. To answer RQ3, we conducted a controlled experiment and obtained quantitative results.
The structure of this paper is as follows: In Section 2, we review the theory and research related to HUDs, SA, and the SRK taxonomy, and present our own conceptual framework. In Section 3, we use the conceptual framework to complete different interface designs. In Sections 4 Methods, 5 Results, we conduct experiments and data analysis. In Section 6, we discuss the results of the experiments. In Section 7, we elaborate on the limitations of this study. Finally, we summarize the work of this study and suggest future work.

2. Context and theoretical framework

In this section, we will review relevant research related to this study, including SA and SRK taxonomy. The SA theory aided us in understanding the information requirements of drivers in the given scenarios, while the SRK taxonomy guided the visualization of information to enhance the driving performance of drivers in hazardous situations.

2.1. AR-HUD related research

Currently, there is a substantial body of research focusing on HUDs. These studies encompass a range of investigations, including comparisons between HUDs and traditional head-down displays (HDDs) concerning their effects on driving capabilities, traffic safety, and driver spatial perception. Additionally, some research has delved into the impact of various types of AR visual elements on a driver’s ability to respond to sudden hazards.
Numerous studies have demonstrated that drivers using HUDs maintain higher driving stability and exhibit quicker responses during the driving process than those using HDDs (e.g., Smith et al., 2016). Bram-Larbi et al. (2020) designed an AI-suggested AR path for a HUD interface. They found that compared to traditional in-car dashboards or central screens, HUDs help emergency vehicle drivers maintain their attention more effectively during traffic congestion, enabling them to perform their tasks more efficiently. In a similar vein, Charissis and Papanastasiou (2010) developed collision signs for HUDs for foggy weather scenarios, featuring size and color variations correlated with distance to enhance driver spatial awareness and response speed in low-visibility conditions. They also tested and verified the effectiveness of HUD in delivering critical information during periods of reduced visibility (Charissis and Papanastasiou, 2006, Charissis et al., 2006).
In research examining the impact of various types of AR visual elements on drivers, Kazazi et al. (2015) and others compared the stop sign warning with three other caution sign warnings, demonstrating that different levels of emergency situations should employ distinct warning types. Different warning types can affect a driver’s speed control and may interact with the driver’s experience in influencing the smoothness of braking (Wu et al., 2018). Chen et al. (2008) and colleagues designed collision prevention features for public buses using AR-HUD, employing icons with different semantics to convey potential collision events and directions. They found that AR visual elements, when accompanied by sound warnings, effectively reduced driver response times to frontal and lateral collision hazards.
In addition to displaying information on AR-HUDs, alternative solutions, such as displaying collision warning patterns in locations such as rear-view mirrors as a substitute for HDD, have been proposed. However, these solutions and design methods lack guidance on how to integrate and express information effectively (Campbell et al., 2007). To enhance effectiveness in scenarios involving pedestrian crossings, Karatas et al. (2020) developed an AR prompt that tracks pedestrians. It was compared to traditional two-dimensional graphical prompts fixed at the bottom of the HUD, demonstrating positive effects on drivers’ ability to recognize pedestrian speed and their acceptance and trust in automatic interventions. Meanwhile, Alves et al. (2013) compared three distance warning prompts on AR-HUDs: a triangular outline indicating close distance, an arrow combination with two colors denoting different danger levels, and an animated arrow combination. However, all three prompts were designed in the traditional two-dimensional graphical form fixed on the HUD screen.

2.2. Situation awareness

SA is the ability to understand the current state of the environment in which one is situated (Jones, 2015). From an individual perspective, SA is defined as “the perception of the elements in the environment within a volume of time and space, the comprehension of their meaning, and the projection of their status in the near future” (Endsley, 1988). Based on this understanding of SA, it can be divided into three levels: perception, comprehension, and projection.
In the face of dangers that appear suddenly or from blind spots in the field of view, or when a driver lacks sufficiently stable visual attention to respond quickly, serious consequences can occur (Smith et al., 2016, Zwahlen et al., 1988). The ADAS, on the other hand, can provide a driver with SA support through an AR-HUD, assisting them in more quickly perceiving potential dangers and preparing for appropriate responses (You et al., 2023). ADAS is being developed and applied to assist drivers in avoiding accidents even when their perception is insufficient or delayed in response. The SA support provided by the system can cover a single level of SA or multiple levels. Therefore, it is extremely important to identify the best ways to encode SA information obtained by the intelligent agent and share it with human drivers. For example, existing in-vehicle human–machine interfaces (HMIs) display warning icons related to different hazardous situations (Nash et al., 2016). However, too many warnings can sometimes increase the driver’s cognitive workload or cause distraction.
With increasingly advanced display technology, information being presented to drivers is not limited to simple sounds and images but can also employ animations or AR to enhance human understanding of the scene. One valuable use of AR messages is to direct the attention of the driver. Medenica et al. (2011) added AR warning information on moving vehicles and other road users to enhance visual effects. AR-HUDs have proven to be good media for providing clues to direct the driver’s attention to hazardous roadside situations, thus improving driving safety (George et al., 2012, Rusch et al., 2013). These studies made us realize that it is important to emphasize key messages in the interface that are consistent with all phases of driver’s SA.
Another important capability of AR-HUDs is conveying predictive information about other traffic participants to drivers. Stange et al. (2022) informed drivers of potential hazards (e.g., pedestrians crossing the road) through an AR-HUD, which increased their trust in autonomous driving systems. Park et al. (2015) presented different information on the AR-HUD to express the level of danger when other vehicles were merging into a lane, and drivers intuitively understood the current situation through AR warning information. AR warning signs can also be used in potential hazard scenarios, such as left-turning vehicle scenarios and predicting collisions at intersections (Calvi et al., 2020, Wu et al., 2019). Kim and Gabbard (2022) investigated the impact of AR elements that gave drivers information on pedestrians crossing the road in different ways on driver distraction. Among them, the virtual shadow element they designed enhanced participants’ awareness of pedestrians without affecting their perception of other road elements. Breve and Zhao (2013) also proposed a vision-based reasoning method that displays information corresponding to three levels of SA on the AR-HUD. This method presented different semantic graphics, providing drivers with recommended driving strategies. This method presented different semantic graphics, providing drivers with recommended driving strategies.
Our research determined some of the SA requirements of drivers in hazardous situations through analytical methods. Interface information content and design followed the characteristics of SA at different levels. We used AR-HUD interface design to deliver information to drivers that is easy to perceive, understand, and predict, thus meeting their SA requirements.

2.3. Skills, Rules, and Knowledge taxonomy (SRK)

After receiving SA information, the driver will provide feedback such as driving decisions based on environmental changes and important information to ensure safe vehicle operation. This cognitive activity is hierarchical and is described by the SRK taxonomy proposed by Danish psychologist (Rasmussen, 1983), which has been widely applied in fields such as aviation and HMI design (Miller, 1988, Miller, 1991).
The SRK taxonomy separates human cognitive activity into three levels: skill-based, rule-based, and knowledge-based (Rasmussen, 1983, Rasmussen, 1987). These three levels correspond to different cognitive processes.

2.3.1. Skill-based behavior

Skill-based behavior is a smooth, automatic, and highly integrated behavioral pattern that is triggered by the driver’s intention state when facing familiar events (Rasmussen, 1987). It refers to skills that can be improved through practice and repeated use. The execution of these skills is automatic and does not require in-depth thinking or decision-making; rather, a certain amount of learning and training is required before mastery can be achieved. For example, skill-based behavior in driving is highly automated (Vicente and Rasmussen, 1988) and represents the driver’s instinctual perception of the vehicle’s motion. When drivers use skill-based behavior for activities, they follow instincts to handle constraints in the road environment and relationships with other traffic participants, such as emergency braking when faced with imminent danger. This type of behavior has a low cognitive load.

2.3.2. Rule-based behavior

Rule-based behavior refers to cognitive activities that can be described by simple rules (Schewe and Vollrath, 2021). These rules can come from everyday experience, professional knowledge, or some kind of norm. At this level, people need to do some thinking and decision-making, but these decisions are usually based on simple rules. For example, stopping at a traffic signal based on the color of the traffic light, etc. (Rasmussen, 1983). Rule-based behavior is a non-automated behavior. First, the driver recognizes the traffic signal, then links it to the driving task state, and finally executes the action based on the known traffic rules. When drivers use rule-based behavior for activities, they need to bear the cognitive load of recognizing and reacting to signals, such as adapting the vehicle speed to the road speed limit (Donges, 1999), by comparing the speedometer display information with the speed limit sign that represents the road rule.

2.3.3. Knowledge-based behavior

Knowledge-based behavior refers to cognitive activities that require in-depth thinking and analysis based on existing knowledge reserves. These activities often involve multiple factors. At this level, people need to integrate different information and knowledge, conduct comprehensive analysis and evaluation, and make final decisions. For example, in driving, knowledge-based behavior involves the driver specifying clear goals (such as the driving route) based on the environment and overall analysis, processing symbols in the environment, understanding and analyzing changes in the situation during task execution, and finally making decisions. Knowledge-based behaviors are thus non-automated behaviors that are triggered when drivers face unfamiliar and non-normal events, and as such have a high cognitive load (Cohen et al., 1990, Miller and Cohen, 2001, Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977).
From the above, it is clear that cognitive activities at different levels correspond to different reaction times. Cognitive activities (and thus reaction times) are also related to the information received from the environment. Therefore, we believe that the interface information of AR-HUDs can be designed to encourage drivers to use skill-based behaviors or rule-based behaviors, thereby accelerating their response time in dangerous situations and improving the efficiency and quality of their cognitive activities.
In design research, there is a concept referred to as the ecological interface, which is also developed based on the SRK taxonomy (Hajdukiewicz and Burns, 2004). AR-HUD information designed with an ecological interface can provide drivers with directly perceivable and easy-to-understand information about the environment and other traffic participants. For example, in a study by Ng-Thow-Hing et al. (2013), to assist drivers in safe left turns, the future path of oncoming vehicles was displayed on the AR-HUD with shape changes that vary with speed. They found that users’ visual attention was primarily focused on the movement of oncoming vehicles and paid little attention to the projected path. In another interface design, they also created a grid box surrounding the ego vehicle on the AR-HUD. The color and transparency of this grid box vary with distance, which to some extent caused drivers to stare continuously. They found that drivers made more frequent lane changes in response to this information, which somewhat inhibited their accurate perception of the situation. The graphical changes in AR can directly affect drivers’ perception of behavior, stimulating drivers’ unconscious, low-workload perception-motion coupling behavior (Schewe and Vollrath, 2020, Schewe and Vollrath, 2021). For example, a speedometer that changes length with the driver’s throttle or brake actions (Schewe and Vollrath, 2020, Schewe and Vollrath, 2021) belongs to a signal that represents spatiotemporal variables. Schall and Gavin (2010) found that using static danger prompts increased drivers’ reaction times compared to no prompts, while dynamic danger-related clues reduced drivers’ reaction times compared to static danger prompts. The variations in the display elements in existing ecological interface designs are solely associated with the driver’s driving behavior. This can occasionally lead to drivers executing incorrect actions to achieve the desired visual effects (Merenda et al., 2018). Furthermore, most of the visualized information has only one meaning.
As with the three types of behaviors mentioned above, studies have shown that dynamic information cues are beneficial for activating drivers’ skill-based behavior. However, the information design in these studies focuses only on variations of a single element, such as shape, color, or semantic variations of a graphic, and does not delve into the question of whether other types of visual information are needed in conjunction with the different phases of a complete event. In our study, we integrated SRK taxonomy and SA to design different information that dynamically changes in shape, color, and semantics for dangerous traffic scenarios.

3. Designing process and conceptual framework

Based on the SRK taxonomy and SA, we proposed an AR-HUD interface design framework and outline the design steps. We will then describe the specific interface design for a given scenario based on this framework and steps. As shown in Fig. 1, the interface design process studied in this paper is based on SA and the SRK taxonomy, which established a framework for designing dynamic spatial information. This was followed by an analysis of cognitive work in hazard scenarios, with adapted use-case diagrams and goal-directed task analysis (GDTA) (Endsley, 2001) to derive SA requirements and specific AR information content for human drivers. Then, the AR information content was visualized for specific scenarios, resulting in an AR-HUD interface visualization form. Finally, the interface design was evaluated through user testing, and based on user feedback, the interface design was iterated to produce the final AR-HUD interface.

3.1. SA requirements analysis

To answer RQ1, we first needed to analyze the SA information involved in the scene. GDTA is commonly used to determine which aspects are important for drivers’ SA in a given scenario (Endsley, 2001). It identifies the SA requirements of decision goals and sub-goals, indicating not only what information the system needs to acquire but also how to combine this information to address these goals. The SA requirements correspond to the dynamic information related to the goals during the task completion process. This dynamic information differs from static information such as knowledge and rules (Endsley, 2001). Endsley and Rodgers (1994) gave an example that showed the SA requirements analysis for an air traffic controller for the sub-goal “Maintain Aircraft Conformance” of the major goal “Avoid Conflictions”. GDTA systematically defines the requirements at three levels of SA and determines how various dynamic information can be combined to form the content that drivers truly want to know. Furthermore, GDTA specifically focuses on dynamic situational information that influences drivers’ behaviors (Endsley, 2001). For drivers, all objects in the traffic environment are considered dynamic situational information, including pedestrians. The three levels of SA refer to the perception of the elements in the environment (level 1), comprehension of the current situation (level 2), and projection of future status (level 3). Therefore, we conducted a GDTA to analyze the goals and tasks involved in the scenario, and to determine the driver’s cognitive information requirements (Endsley, 2001).
As shown in Fig. 2, in the dangerous driving scenario, the driver’s overall goal is safe driving. Under the overall goal, there are three sub-goals, namely: monitoring vehicle status, controlling the vehicle, and observing road conditions. Under the overall goal, there are three sub-goals: monitoring vehicle status, controlling the vehicle, and observing road conditions. Under the first sub-goal, the driver’s SA requirements are current position (SA level 1), current speed (SA level 1), environmental limitations (SA level 2), speed limitations, and displacement trend (SA level 3). Under the second sub-goal, the driver’s SA requirements are potential hazards (SA level 1), other traffic participants’ intentions (SA level 2), and the impact of actions (SA level 3). In a study conducted by Merenda et al. (2018), different driving tasks were categorized as goal-directed tasks and stimulus-driven tasks. Events like pedestrians suddenly crossing the driving path require drivers to engage in stimulus-driven tasks, where they cannot anticipate what will happen and can only react based on the changing situation (Merenda et al., 2018). The third sub-goal, observing road conditions, can be considered as a task objective within stimulus-driven tasks. To accomplish such a task objective, drivers typically employ a bottom-up processing information pattern. Under this sub-goal, the driver’s SA requirements are safety status (SA level 1), danger level (SA level 2), and changes in condition (SA level 3).

3.2. Identify SA elements

After identifying the SA information required by human drivers, we need to deduce the related SA information that can be provided by the ADAS. In this paper, ADAS specifically refers to an information visualization system that helps the driver to perceive hazards as well as better avoid them. This system provides visual information assistance to the driver via an AR-HUD (WSD) under manual driving conditions. The information that drivers need can be obtained through a use case diagram (Jacobson, 1993), which can be used to establish the relationship between different system functions and the different task goals of drivers (Marshall, 1992). As shown in Fig. 3, in a manual driving scenario, the driver has specific driving goals and corresponding SA requirements. The ADAS provides information to the driver through its various information modules to support the driver’s SA.
The abstract goals, tasks, and functions of both the driver and the vehicle system are:
  • •
    Human: The overall goal is safe driving, which can be divided into three sub-goals: vehicle status monitoring, observation of road conditions, and vehicle control. To achieve these goals, the driver must perform tasks such as speed control, hazard perception, and hazard assessment when facing sudden dangerous situations. Real-time information such as vehicle speed, road speed limit, road conditions, and the behaviors of other traffic participants is required by the driver.
  • •
    ADAS: Includes a lane departure warning system, collision avoidance system, and/or pre-collision system. These functionalities are supported by in-vehicle end-user computing units, along with sensors such as millimeter-wave radar and single or dual cameras serving as video sensors. The detection range of these sensors spans 30–150 m. When the vehicle is traveling at speeds ranging from 20–70 km/h, with no turn signals activated, a steering wheel rotation angle of less than 5 degrees, and hazard lights off, the system conducts an analysis considering the distance to other vehicles and relative speeds. Based on this analysis, when a collision risk is identified, it presents visual warning alerts via an AR-HUD (WSD). Consequently, in this scenario, the primary objective of the ADAS is collision prevention. To enable the driver to manage vehicle speed effectively, discern the intentions of other traffic participants, and avoid hazards, support from information modules like speed limit warning, blind spot detection, side collision warning, and front collision warning is indispensable. These information modules provide functionalities such as signal detection, orientation detection, distance measurement, speed detection, and blind spot detection. These functions collectively provide information to the driver, enhancing the driver’s SA.
Through the adapted use-case diagram, we can identify that there are four pieces of information that collision warning systems can provide to drivers: speed limit, current speed, relationship with other traffic participants, and other traffic participants’ behaviors. These four pieces of information meet the shared SA requirements of the human–vehicle team during general driving and even in dangerous situations.

3.3. Dynamic Spatial Information Design (DSID)

To answer RQ2, we needed to convert the information obtained from Sections 3.1 SA requirements analysis, 3.2 Identify SA elements into dynamic spatial information. To achieve this, we needed to understand the types of information that trigger different levels of driver behaviors and match the interface information content accordingly. According to the SRK taxonomy, there are three types of information used to trigger human skill-based, rule-based, and knowledge-based behaviors: signal, sign, and symbol, respectively. The definitions of these three types of information are shown in Table 1.
In hazardous driving scenarios, accidents occur when drivers fail to manage their relationship with other traffic participants and have insufficient time to complete the cognitive process of understanding symbols. Based on the above three types of information, the most important information in dangerous traffic situations should be dynamic spatial information, which needs to be designed in terms of semantics, shape, and color so that the information changes continuously in time and space, and the driver’s skill-based behavior can be mapped to the continuous changes in the information.
Fig. 4 illustrates the transformation of the three types of information in our DSID framework, taking the design of lane departure warning as an example. The ADAS obtains situational perception elements from the environment and visualizes them, which are transmitted to the driver through the AR-HUD. The information transmitted to the driver by AR-HUD may be symbol, sign, or signal.

Symbol-type information often appears in conventional driver vehicle interfaces and can be designed as either screen-fixed or world-fixed representations (Gabbard et al., 2014). In the example of a lane departure warning, if the system only displays a red lane and vehicle combination icon, this type of visual information falls under the category of symbol. This type of information requires the driver to rely on their prior life experience and knowledge to infer its meaning of lane departure. At this point, the driver also needs to perceive the specific situation in the actual environment (i.e., which direction the vehicle is departing from the lane) and then adjust the vehicle’s driving state to eliminate the warning. If multiple attempts fail to eliminate the warning (i.e., change the visual information being provided on the AR-HUD), the driver will be confused and suspect that the system function has failed. This could lead to drivers ignoring such warnings in the future.
If the system displays an icon representing the warning that the vehicle is deviating from the lane to the left, this visual information is classified as a sign. At this time, the driver steers the vehicle to the right based on the meaning expressed by the sign and restores the appropriate position. Nowadays, the vast majority of lane departure warnings are designed as animated signs; that is, the lateral displacement of the vehicle corresponds to the movement of the vehicle in the visualization. Sign-type information not only appears on the current conventional driver-vehicle interface using screen-fixed and screen-animated representation methods but will also be present on future AR-HUDs using the world-fixed representation method after undergoing conformal design approaches (Merenda et al., 2018).
However, the driver still needs to go through the coordinate system conversion from the graphical interface to the real space when dealing with this type of sign warning, which is why signal warnings are often preferable. The nature of signal-type information itself determines that it is best represented using the world-fixed or world-animated methods (Merenda et al., 2018). If the lane departure warning is designed as dynamic spatial information, it can directly help the driver perform an appropriate skill-based behavior. The AR dynamic driving area superimposed on the road will change with the control of the steering wheel by the driver. The lane departure situation will be intuitively displayed in the real driving space. Then, the driver would not need to perform additional spatial coordinate system conversion; they would only need to adjust the steering wheel to keep the AR dynamic driving space in the lane of the real environment to complete the task of remaining in their lane.
In complex traffic environments, not all pieces of information are amenable to a single design approach for expression. Therefore, AR-HUDs (WSD) provide visual information using various design methods. For instance, they may superimpose path guidance on the actual road, utilizing either the world-fixed or world-animated approach, while simultaneously presenting the current road speed limit value in a screen-animated format. The interface elements from each design approach can be meaningfully combined and presented on the AR-HUD (WSD) (Merenda et al., 2018). Therefore, we do not intend to confine ourselves to a specific interface design approach or to a particular level of information type within the SRK taxonomy in our design.

3.4. Designing HMI

3.4.1. Scenario and cognitive task analysis

In this study, we selected the dangerous scenario (see Fig. 5) where the ego car and the right-turning vehicle encounter at an intersection without traffic lights. In fact, intersection-related accidents account for about 20%–45% of all reported traffic accidents in developed and developing countries (Ma et al., 2021, Golembiewski et al., 2011). In all intersections (including uncontrolled intersections) of China, vehicles making a right turn followed by a straight movement are supposed to yield to vehicles traveling straight through the intersection. In the research scenario of this study, according to the rules, the participants’ vehicles were consistently traveling straight, so they were not required to yield. However, non-compliance with traffic rules by other road users often leads to highly dangerous situations. Without the guidance of traffic lights, yielding between vehicles relies solely on understanding other vehicles’ intentions. However, this is a higher-level cognitive behavior based on knowledge and rules, and drivers must pay a high cognitive load in predicting other vehicles’ intention-related cues (Cooper et al., 2003). At this point, drivers may have difficulty processing the information in the scene in a timely manner based on the knowledge and rule hierarchy, leading to an inability to use appropriate skill-based behaviors to avoid danger, which may result in serious accidents (Engström and Markkula, 2007).
To effectively apply the SRK taxonomy to the design of the AR-HUD interface, we not only consider the human user’s mental model, but also the machine’s information acquisition and processing patterns. We adopted the theory proposed by Parasuraman et al. (2000), which identifies four functions of automation: information acquisition, information analysis, decision-making, and action execution. Based on the level of automation in manual driving, we adjusted these automation functions and mapped them to the cognitive and behavioral stages of human drivers. We analyzed the driving tasks in the hazardous scenario involving the Ego car and the turning vehicle at an intersection without traffic lights using the analytical method mentioned in Sections 3.1 SA requirements analysis, 3.2 Identify SA elements, as shown in Fig. 6.
We present below the details of the information processing stages in which human drivers and vehicle information systems are involved during driving tasks.
  • •
    Driver: State 1: In the perception stage (SA level 1), the SA demands are current speed, safety status, and potential hazards. State 2: In the comprehension stage (SA level 2), the SA demands are speed limit, danger level, and other vehicles’ intentions. State 3: In the projection stage (SA level 3), the SA demands are situation changes and the impacts of actions. State 4: In the decision-making stage, the driver takes the action of decelerating to avoid danger.
  • •
    ADAS: State 1: In the information acquisition stage, speed detection, blind spot detection, and collision detection are performed, which can provide easily perceivable information to the driver (easily perceivable information may be prominent warning). State 2: In the information analysis stage, analysis of speed limits, collision possibilities, and other traffic participants’ behaviors is provided to the driver in a way that is easy to understand and helps them to predict changes in the situation. State 3: In the feedback stage, the current dynamic dangerous situation is visualized through AR-HUD.

3.4.2. Design schemes

Based on the design framework introduced in Section 3.3 and the analysis of cognitive tasks in the aforementioned scenario, the next step is to design an information display for our AR-HUD interface. According to the driver’s information needs, the system must recognize and display the situation of the road ahead while driving forward.
In general, our approach to designing the AR-HUD interface with the DSID framework begins with a flat presentation, then progresses to a semi-spatial presentation, and finally culminates in spatializing the information.
  • •
    Flat presentation: In this stage, all driver information requirements and corresponding functional information are presented in a traditional two-dimensional format on the interface. At this point, all the information is temporarily represented in a screen-fixed or screen-animated format. ADAS must provide both lane- and speed-related cues to the driver while conveying dynamic hazard situations and early warning information.
  • •
    Semi-spatial presentation: Since drivers have a strong demand to view early warnings, speed, and dynamic hazard information, and they need to slow down, prioritizing the spatial representation optimization of these pieces of information becomes crucial. This stage also involves transitioning information from the knowledge-based level to the other two levels. Therefore, the design strategy at this stage is to position warning information in the direction of the impending danger and represent the deceleration effect and dynamic hazard changes on the forward road. The remaining information can retain the forms used in the previous stage.
  • •
    Information spatialization: Designers need to integrate and optimize the semi-spatial information to avoid redundancy. For instance, warnings can appear well in advance when approaching an intersection and disappear when dynamic hazard situations emerge. Dynamic hazard situations and deceleration effects should be intuitively represented on the forward road. Combining conclusions or design recommendations from existing studies, such as the effectiveness of world-animated forms in capturing attention compared to two fixed methods, or the use of animations independent of vehicle motion to convey real-world dangers, and the rapid attention-guiding ability of fixed-world conformal graphics (Merenda et al., 2018), designers can then employ dynamic changes in the shape of the driving space on the road to convey deceleration effects, as well as color and coverage area changes to represent dynamic hazard situations. This completes the process of translating key information into the skill-based level.
The dynamic driving space on the road ahead is often displayed in green, indicating a clear and safe road. When a nearby vehicle is detected that may cause danger, the AR-HUD will display a yellow triangular warning symbol to guide the driver’s attention to the dangerous area. We then correspond the change in the distance between the cars in the danger situation with the change in the area of the red zone, where red is also the semantic for danger. Such a change is consistent with the definition that dynamic spatial information changes continuously in space and time with the environment. To map the driver’s skill-based behavior to continuous changes in the spatial and temporal attributes of the information, we make the length of the dynamic driving area vary with the degree of braking by the driver. At the same time, the length of the dynamic driving space also represents the expected braking distance of the vehicle. In this way, the driver can intuitively understand the changes in the distance between vehicles, the degree of danger, and the impact of speed control behavior in the current driving environment from the representation of the dynamic driving space.
Fig. 7 depicts four AR-HUD (WSD) interfaces, HMI1–HMI4. Both HMI1 and HMI2 employ the DSID for the AR dynamic driving space. The dynamic driving space visualizes the real-time situation of the road ahead, showing green when the road is safe and gradually being covered in red as danger approaches. The area and rate of change of the red region correspond to the level of danger. The longitudinal length of the dynamic driving space changes as the driver slows down the vehicle, which reflects the expected braking distance of the vehicle. The visual mapping of such information is aimed at activating the driver’s behavior pattern based on skill hierarchy, helping them use automatic skills to avoid danger quickly and appropriately. HMI2 has an additional feature of providing early warnings of oncoming side vehicles before entering the intersection, 2.5 s in advance (Srinivasa, 2002, Nakaoka et al., 2008), compared to HMI1.
HMI3 and HMI4 both utilize a quasi-DSID. The quasi-dynamic driving space is typically displayed in green in a safe state. When the danger approaches to a certain degree, the quasi-dynamic driving space changes from green to red. As the situation changes and the driver moves away from the dangerous condition, the status of the quasi-dynamic driving space switches back from red to green. Besides the common quasi-dynamic driving space element, HMI4 also has an advance warning of lateral traffic 2.5 s before entering a crossroads (Srinivasa, 2002, Nakaoka et al., 2008), while HMI3 does not.
To provide a clear and concise description of the characteristics of the four design schemes, we will refer to the dynamic driving space in HMI1 and HMI2 as Dynamic Spatial Information (DSI), and the quasi-dynamic driving space in HMI3 and HMI4 as Quasi-Dynamic Spatial Information (QDSI). The lateral warning will be referred to as LW, and these designations will be indicated in parentheses when mentioning the four design schemes.

4. Methods

4.1. Experimental design

4.1.1. Hypotheses

The purpose of this research is to explore the impacts of the four different forms of dynamic information design mentioned in Section 3.4.2 on driver SA and performance in dangerous situations (RQ3). We propose the following hypotheses:
H1: DSID can help enhance drivers’ SA and improve driving performance.
H2: DSID can reduce drivers’ reaction times.

4.1.2. Independent variables

We used a paired repeated measures experimental design. The experiment’s independent variables were the four AR-HUD interface designs. Table 2 shows in detail the differences in information types between the four schemes.

Table 2. Demonstration graphs of the four augmented conditions and comparison of the four design schemes and three types of information.
