HMI2YesYesYes
HMI3NoYesNo
HMI4YesYesNo

4.1.3. Dependent variables and measurements

The dependent variables examined in this experiment were eye-tracking data, driving performance, usability, cognitive workload, and SA, in consideration of the two hypotheses.
  • 1.
    Average fixation duration, number of fixations, average visit duration, and number of visits: We established two areas of interest (AOI) (Fig. 8), one for the lane region directly ahead and the other for the area where the side warning messages are located. The experiment measured the driver’s average duration of fixation, number of fixations, average visit duration, and number of visits to these areas of interest.
  • 2.
    Driving performance: Driving performance comprises the driver’s decision time, acceleration at the moment of decision, and the value of deceleration. We use the acceleration at the moment of the driver’s avoidance decision and the deceleration value of the vehicle within 1 s afterwards as a measure of the driver’s driving performance. The decision time in the experiment begins when the patient’s vehicle passes the trigger we established in the scene (for triggering the oncoming car on the right); the decision time ends when the driver executes the avoidance action. In addition, rapid acceleration and deceleration are high-risk driving behaviors that are commonly regarded as unsafe and highly correlated with the occurrence of accidents (Zhu et al., 2017). The identification of rapid acceleration and deceleration events is often performed based on fixed thresholds, and for various research purposes, 2.94 to 3.92 m/s2 is a common judgment threshold (Bergasa et al., 2014, Hong et al., 2014, Toledo et al., 2008, Paefgen et al., 2012).
  • 3.
    The after-scenario questionnaire (ASQ) (Lewis, 1991) is a commonly used task-based assessment questionnaire that evaluates system usability in terms of ease of task completion, time necessary to complete the task, and satisfaction with supporting information. The options for the scale questions range from 1 to 7, with higher scores indicating more usability, and the final ASQ score is the mean of the three values on the scale.
  • 4.
    Workload: The driving activity load index (DALI) (Pauzié, 2008) is a driving-specific modification of the NASA-TLX. The DALI is based on the same fundamental principle as the TLX. In both tools, a scale scoring mechanism is provided for six preset parameters, followed by a weighting procedure to aggregate the six distinct scales into an overall score. The scale options range from 1 to 10, and the final score is calculated using a weighting method.
  • 5.
    Situation Awareness: The situation awareness rating technique (SART) (Selcon and Taylor, 1990, Taylor, 2017) is a simple subjective post-test rating scale containing 10 SA dimensions: instability of situation, complexity of situation, variability of situation, arousal, concentration of attention, division of attention, spare mental capacity, information quantity, and familiarity with situation. The participants completed the scale following the experiment. Participants scored each dimension on a 7-point scale depending on their sentiments and task performance (1 = low, 7 = high). Finally, these scores were merged to assess the participants’ SA.

4.2. Experiment

4.2.1. Participants

We recruited 20 participants with valid driver’s licenses and normal or corrected vision through online platforms. All participants were briefed about the context of our study, both during the recruitment process and after they arrived at our experimental site. The average age of the participants was 29.7 years (SD = 6.36), and their average driving experience was 6.4 years (SD = 6.20). All participants were from Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, China, and included students, white-collar workers, and blue-collar workers. Each participant signed an informed consent form before participating in the experiment, and the average duration of their participation was approximately 30 min. They were provided with detailed information about the experiment and were compensated for their time and participation.

4.2.2. Apparatus

The experiment was conducted in a virtual driving simulation environment in our laboratory. The experimental environment consists of a fixed-base driving simulator, a primary driving system, and an experimental monitoring system. The fixed-base driving simulator and primary driving system are located in the experimental area’s center, while the experimental monitoring system was located on the left side of the driving simulator, parallel to the front of the simulator. The experimental setting was encircled by soundproof panels to limit outside disturbance during the experiment.
In this experiment, a virtual driving scenario was created using Unity2 software and exhibited on three 55-inch monitors with a resolution of 3840 × 2160. The Tobii Glasses 2 Head Unit (serial: TG02G-010117936884) was utilized to record the eye-movement data of the individuals. Using the associated Tobii Pro Lab3 software, the eye-movement data were analyzed (see Fig. 9).

4.2.3. Procedure

This experiment required participants to maintain a consistent velocity of 40 km/h in both directions on a two-lane city street. During this period, the participants traveled through an intersection. Various components, including sounds, sidewalks, street trees, city buildings, and so on were arranged in the driving simulator setting so that the participants would have a natural and realistic driving experience. In addition, participants did not always experience exactly the same situations, as our scenario settings have a certain degree of randomness. The vehicles driven by the participants may encounter right-turning vehicles from the right side at the intersection, or the right-turning vehicles may have already passed before the participants reached the intersection. Moreover, if the participants do not encounter right-turning vehicles during their first pass at the intersection, they will definitely encounter this dangerous situation at the next intersection. We emphasized with each participant that we expected them to decelerate to avoid sudden dangerous situations with the assistance of the information presented via the AR-HUD (WSD) interface.
Each participant was fitted with the eye-tracking device at the beginning of the experiment, and the device was calibrated using single-point calibration mode. Adjusting the height of the nose pads of the device facilitated a more pleasant wearing experience for the individual. During the experiment, the experimenter observed the participant’s perspective on a Windows Surface tablet equipped with the eye-tracking recording software.
Prior to the start of the experiment, all participants were given the opportunity to experience our simulated driving simulator in a virtual driving scenario similar to the formal experiment. Participants must be somewhat familiar with using the driving simulator to manage the vehicle in a virtual setting, including speed control and directional control, because operating a driving simulator differs from driving a real vehicle in numerous ways. They were therefore also familiarized with the visual representation of information in AR-HUD through the use of interface designs from existing studies. Each participant was provided with an explanation of the graphical information variations in our designed interface, ensuring that they had a base level of familiarity with our AR-HUD interface.
After familiarization was completed, the participants began completing the experimentally determined driving task, utilizing various AR-HUD interfaces (see Fig. 7). The Latin square design was applied to counterbalance the order of interface design schemes. When a participant completed a driving activity utilizing one of the AR-HUD interfaces, the subject was asked to complete the ASQ, SART, and DALI scales.

5. Results

In this experiment, we performed data testing using SPSS 26.0 software. GraphPad Prism was utilized to visually represent the results. The measured values of each indicator were not normally distributed, as indicated by the Shapiro–Wilk test (Shapiro and Wilk, 1965). To evaluate the four AR-HUD interface scenarios, a nonparametric test based on the Friedman test (Friedman, 1937) was employed. After finding significant differences between the samples, post hoc multiple comparisons were performed using the Bonferroni–Dunn test. Furthermore, all results were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni correction during data analysis. The median (Mdn) with the first quartile (Q1) and the third quartile (Q3) of each variable was presented as Mdn = median (Q1, Q3).

5.1. Driving performance

A total of 20 drivers participated in this experiment. Each driver experienced all four AR-HUD design schemes. Due to a program bug, one subject’s data was not recorded completely, so we excluded this participant’s data.
The results of the participants’ decision times when utilizing the four AR-HUD interfaces are depicted in Fig. 10(a). The shorter the decision time, the more effective the interface design solution. The Friedman test revealed a statistically significant difference (p = 0.009) between the effects of the four HMIs on the participants’ decision time. Post hoc multiple comparison analysis (Bonferroni–Dunn test) revealed that the participants’ decision time was significantly shorter with HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 3.23 (2.59, 3.70)) than with HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 3.82 (3.39, 4.17), p = 0.0031), HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 3.74 (3.24, 4.35), p = 0.0049), and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 3.96 (3.23, 4.22), p = 0.0028). The decision time for HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) was slightly shorter than that for HMI4 (QDSI, LW), while the decision time for HMI1 (DSI, no LW) was slightly longer than that for HMI4 (QDSI, LW), but neither was significantly different (p > 0.05).
Fig. 10(b) depicts the acceleration of the vehicle at the moment of participants’ decision when utilizing the four AR-HUD interfaces. The smaller the absolute acceleration values, the gentler the deceleration behavior, and the more closely the absolute acceleration values approach 0.3–0.4 g (g = 9.80 m/s2), the more efficient the interface design solution. The Friedman test revealed that the four HMIs had statistically varied effects on the acceleration of individuals at the time of decision (p = 0.002). Post hoc multiple comparison analysis revealed that the absolute acceleration of participants using HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 4.03 (3.17, 6.10)) was the closest to the tolerable deceleration threshold and was significantly different from HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 8.28 (5.54, 22.84), p = 0.003) and HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 8.71 (4.53, 20.51), p = 0.003). HMI2 (DSI, LW) was marginally superior to HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 6.52 (3.62, 9.96)), but not significantly (p = 0.435). The acceleration of HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) was less than that of HMI1 (DSI, no LW), and the acceleration of HMI1 (DSI, no LW) was less than that of HMI4 (QDSI, LW), although neither difference was statistically significant (p > 0.05).
Fig. 10(c) shows the results of deceleration when using the four AR-HUD interfaces. On the premise of no collision, the smaller deceleration value proves the milder the deceleration behavior and the more effective the interface design scheme. The Friedman test revealed a statistically significant difference (p = 0.002) in the effects of the four HMIs on deceleration. The participants’ deceleration with HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 7.00 (5.80, 9.80)) was the smallest and significantly different from HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 12.00 (7.30, 14.60), p = 0.003) and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 12.80 (7.90, 14.40), p = 0.008). HMI2 (DSI, LW) was marginally better than HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 11.80 (6.90, 14.30)), but not significantly (p = 0.061). The deceleration of HMI4 (QDSI, LW) was less than that of HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) and less than that of HMI1 (DSI, no LW), although neither difference was statistically significant (p > 0.05).

5.2. Subjective scales

Fig. 11(a) displays the results of the SART scale. Higher SART scores indicate a participant with better SA and interface solutions. The Friedman test confirmed that the four AR-HUD interfaces had significantly distinct effects on the SA of the subjects (p = 0.001). Dunn’s multiple comparison analysis revealed that HMI2 (DSI, LW) had the highest median SART score (Mdn = 27.50 (24.00, 31.75)) compared to both HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 21.00 (15.00, 26.00), p = 0.001) and HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 22.00 (14.25, 27.00)) significantly (p = 0.014). The difference between the median SART scores of HMI2 (DSI, LW) and HMI4 was not statistically significant (p = 0.402). The difference between the SART scores of HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 23.50 (21.00, 27.00)) and HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) and HMI1 (DSI, no LW) was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). The median SART score of HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) was slightly higher than that of HMI1 (DSI, no LW), again not significant (p > 0.05).
Fig. 11(b) displays the results of the ASQ scale scores. Higher ASQ scores suggest a more usable solution. The Friedman test showed that the four AR-HUD interfaces had significantly distinct effects on ASQ ratings (p = 0.0001). Post hoc multiple comparisons revealed that HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 6.00 (5.42, 6.68)) had the highest ASQ score when compared to HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 4.833 (4.33, 5.33), p = 0.001), HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 4.833 (4.08, 5.00), p = 0.001), and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 5.333 (4.67, 6.00), p = 0.006). The difference between the ASQ scores of HMI4 and HMI1 (DSI, no LW) was not statistically significant (p = 0.345). The difference between the ASQ scores of HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) and HMI1 (DSI, no LW) was again not statistically significant (p = 1.000).
Fig. 11(c) shows the results of the DALI scale. The lower the DALI score, the lighter the participant’s cognitive workload and the superior the interface solution. The Friedman test indicated that the impacts of the four AR-HUD interfaces on the DALI scores were significantly different (p = 0.0002). Post hoc multiple comparison analysis revealed that HMI2 (DSI, LW) had the lowest DALI score (Mdn = 48.75 (35.21, 64.79)) and this difference was statistically significant (p<0.05) when compared to both HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 89.58 (47.08, 115.20), p = 0.01) and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 76.25 (50.21, 95.62), p = 0.035). The difference between the DALI scores of HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 69.58 (42.29, 116.70)) and HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) was not statistically significant (p = 0.482). The difference between the DALI scores of HMI1 (DSI, no LW) and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) was not statistically significant (p > 0.05).

5.3. Eye-tracking data

Eye-tracking data can reflect the attention distribution of drivers in the driving process to some extent. On the premise that most accidents can be effectively avoided, the participants’ average duration of fixation, number of fixations, and average visit duration for the front AOI are low, indicating that the information in the front AOI does not distract the driver’s attention excessively and can assist the driver in detecting the presence of potential hazards. As for the side AOI, the high values of these indicators mentioned above indicates that the interface solution can—to some extent—effectively guide the driver’s attention to the side hazards, which is helpful to compensate for the driver’s usual (unassisted) lack of side attention.
Fig. 12 displays the results for the fixation duration for each of the two AOIs (in milliseconds). The Friedman test revealed that the influence of the four AR-HUD interfaces on the fixation time of the front AOI was not significantly different (p > 0.05), but the effect on the fixation duration of the side AOI was significantly different (p = 0.003). According to the statistical description, the fixation time on the front AOI was shortest for HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 259.80 (190.00, 379.80)). The fixation time on the side AOI was greater for HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 208.00 (163.80, 235.10)) than for HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 143.00 (104.00, 197.40), p = 0.009) with significant and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 146.00 (105.60, 204.90)), but less than for HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 219.90 (184.20, 268.20)). The fixation time on the side AOI was greater for HMI2 (DSI, LW) compared to HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) with significant (p = 0.003) and also significant (p = 0.009) compared to HMI4 (QDSI, LW). The gaze time for the side AOI in HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) was lower than in HMI4 (QDSI, LW).
The results for the number of AOI fixation points are displayed in Fig. 13. The Friedman test demonstrated that the number of AOI fixation points across the various AR-HUD interfaces did not differ significantly (p > 0.05). HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 4.0 (3.0, 6.0)) exhibited the lowest number of fixation points for AOI on the road ahead, followed by HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 5.0 (1.5, 7.0)), HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 4.5 (3.0, 7.75)), and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 5.0 (2.25, 7.0)). HMI2 (DSI, LW) (Mdn = 1.5 (1.0, 2.0)) had the largest number of fixation points for the side AOI, followed by HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 0.5 (0, 2.0)) and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 1.0 (0, 1.75)), which were both more than HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 0 (0, 1.0)).
Fig. 14 displays the results of the visit duration for two AOIs (in milliseconds) . The Friedman test revealed that the duration for participants to visit the front AOI was not statistically different across the AR-HUD interfaces (p > 0.05), but the time for participants to visit the side AOI was significant (p = 0.026). According to the statistical description, the visit duration of the front AOI was longer for HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 786.2 (276.5, 1334.0)) than for HMI1 (DSI, no LW) (Mdn = 699.6 (413.1, 1084.0)) and HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 520.8 (271.7, 878.2)), while the visit time was longer for HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) than for HMI1 (DSI, no LW). Post hoc multiple comparison analysis revealed that the visit duration of the side AOI was significantly longer (p = 0.029) for HMI2 (Mdn = 232.8 (187.7, 337.9)) than for HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) (Mdn = 176.1 (137.7, 223.1)). The visit duration to the side AOI when drivers used HMI4 (QDSI, LW) (Mdn = 177.9 (140.5, 236.1)) was longer than HMI3 (QDSI, no LW), but less than HMI1 (DSI, no LW).

6. Discussion

Based on the SRK taxonomy and SA theory, this paper proposes a DSID framework for AR-HUD interfaces in hazardous intersection scenarios and presents four design interfaces. The research first addresses what SA information needs to be shared with the human driver through the interface in the hazard scenario (RQ1) and what method should be used to design a DSI that meets drivers’ SA needs (RQ2). In the experimental study, we compared four AR-HUD interfaces with different forms of dynamic information and varying levels of informational content to determine the impacts of different forms of dynamic information design on drivers’ behavior (RQ3).
From our analyses of the driving performance data and subjective rating scores, it was clear that HMI2 with DSID and lateral warnings provided drivers with the highest level of SA and usability, and the lowest workload; HMI2 also resulted in the best driving performance among the four interfaces. This finding supports H1, indicating that well-designed DSID can enhance drivers’ SA and improve their driving performance.
HMI3 (QDSI, no LW) and HMI4 (QDSI, LW) both adopted quasi-DSID, but with a lateral warning, HMI4 was slightly better than HMI3. Although HMI1 (DSI, no LW) also adopted DSID, its lack of lateral warning made it inferior to HMI2 (DSI, LW), supporting the hypothesis that DSID can reduce driver’s reaction time (H2). From these experimental results, we found that AR-HUD interfaces combining warnings with DSID were most effective at enhancing drivers’ driving performance and SA in dangerous scenarios.

6.1. Warning

For the purpose of safe driving, drivers are required to slow down and check for any oncoming vehicles or pedestrians when approaching an intersection. Once it is confirmed to be safe, the driver can proceed through the intersection. According to traffic regulations in China, vehicles making turns should yield to vehicles going straight. Therefore, most drivers rely on their knowledge of this regulation to prepare for potential hazards when approaching an intersection. Although this means that drivers are utilizing a knowledge-based processing mode to handle information, which is slower than a skill-based processing mode, the early appearance of warnings via an AR-HUD can help drivers prepare psychologically for the danger.
Comparative studies on symbols and alphanumeric data within HUDs have indicated that human recognition of symbols is significantly faster than text recognition (Shekhar et al., 1991). Despite interrupting the continuous safe state and temporarily releasing drivers from the control loop of dynamic driving tasks (Kaber and Endsley, 1997, Michon, 1985, Ranney, 1994), a concise 2D warning symbol effectively supports the perception stage of drivers’ SA, helping drivers quickly perceive danger.
In our design, lateral warnings are implemented using the conformal design approach, presented in a world-fixed manner. Conformal design has been demonstrated to have positive effects on directing drivers’ attention and performance (Kim and Gabbard, 2022, Smith et al., 2021). In our HMIs, warnings appear before the driver enters an intersection, at a point when the driver has not yet encountered a vehicle rapidly approaching from the side (i.e., before entering a stimulus-driven task scenario). At this stage, precise attention to the right-front intersection behavior is not required, and the use of world-fixed cues can quickly guide the driver’s attention to potential hazards (Merenda et al., 2018, Smith et al., 2021). Furthermore, warnings located in real space allow the driver to comprehend the information and its position without the need for additional spatial mapping processes, such as coordinating transformations between flat and spatial coordinate systems (Tönnis et al., 2009). Additionally, the use of simple graphics during the driving process can rapidly capture spatial attention, enabling the driver to selectively process visual information by prioritizing a specific area within their field of view (Karatas et al., 2020). Our experimental findings on warning information are consistent with previous research that simple graphics easily convey information to drivers, enhancing perception (Merenda et al., 2018).
Participants’ statistical eye-tracking data showed that the average fixation and visit durations for the lateral warning information in HMI2 (DSI, LW) were significantly longer than in the other three HMIs. Research suggests that AR information may not actually improve drivers’ perception of real-world maneuver cues, but instead influences the allocation of visual attention by increasing fixations and reducing task specificity (Eyraud et al., 2015). Moreover, longer fixations or dwell times do not necessarily indicate effective attention guidance; longer fixations may indicate that the driver is stuck in an attention tunnel or does not comprehend the graphical information. In our demonstration scenario, the lateral warning appears before the approach of the side vehicle, and its disappearance aligns with the start of color change in the DSI on the forward road, reducing the likelihood of attention tunneling. Additionally, due to the limited time available for drivers to respond to danger, there were no excessively long fixation or visitation times. Future research should further investigate the impact of lateral warnings on drivers’ attention in real driving scenarios.

6.2. Dynamic spatial information

Our designed DSI is attached to the road ahead, and its content changes with the driver’s behavior and situation, visualizing the relative motion positions and states between vehicles, which may help drivers establish accurate mental models (Kim and Gabbard, 2022). The dynamic changes in semantics, color, and graphic shape of the DSI conform to human behavior classification and the definition of signals at the skill-based level of the SRK taxonomy. DSI consists of an expanding red area that is independent of vehicle speed and distance traveled. As observed by Karatas et al. (2020), when the AR-HUD interface explicitly and dynamically presents hazardous objects rather than relying on metaphors or static indicators, drivers are able to identify targets more rapidly. This animation provides crucial spatial cues about the hazard and also offers predictions about the hazard’s future development (Merenda et al., 2018).
According to our eye-tracking data, the average fixation time, number of fixations, and average visit duration of the participants using HMI2 (DSI, LW) are slightly less than the other three HMIs. To some extent, this represents the spatiotemporal variables of the dynamic spatial structure, which can be perceived by humans as continuous variables and thus activate drivers’ behavior based on skills. DSI may also shorten the time for the driver to understand spatial information by supporting the driver’s understanding of the spatiotemporal structure of the scene. Furthermore, drivers may not have to rely on high-level knowledge, experience, and reasoning to take action, thus potentially preserving more attentional resources and cognitive capacity for other elements in the environment (Bennett and Flach, 2011, Merenda et al., 2018).
DSI assists drivers’ decision-making rather than replacing it, and the benefit is that it does not cause significant conflicts between interface information and drivers’ mental models and SA when processing dangerous situations. In their study on the effects of the animation and boundary design of an AR-HUD’s visual elements on driver attention and driving performance, Wang et al. (2023) et al. concluded that animation and boundary design have a positive impact on visual detection time. Additionally, with non-animated warnings, boundaries also positively affect brake reaction time. These experimental results, as well as the advantages of our HMI2 (DSI, LW) in average decision-making time and driving behavior mildness, provide support for this point. Dynamic cues have also been demonstrated in existing studies to reduce drivers’ reaction times (Eyraud et al., 2015). Our DSID is different from previous designs that only had dynamic changes in color, semantics, or external shape in some aspects, and uses different visualization methods for other vehicle behaviors than were employed in previous designs.
In summary, the simple visual appearance of the lateral warning does not compete for excessive attentional resources with real-world objects, thereby facilitating drivers’ reactions to danger in emergency situations. DSI, compared to traditional screen-fixed or world-fixed conformal cues, utilizes a world-animated approach that incorporates both directional and motion-based cues. This approach supports accurate spatial judgments to a certain extent, activating drivers’ automatic sensor-motion mode and enabling them to decelerate and maneuver appropriately with a lower cognitive load when facing hazardous situations.
However, using AR graphics designed solely with the world- animated approach did not lead to the best driver performance, possibly because the drivers were required to come to a sudden stop, while the AR graphics continued to display ongoing animations. To some extent, this may lead drivers to focus solely on AR graphics without paying attention to actual road conditions (Smith et al., 2020). However, the early appearance of simple world-fixed AR graphics, as opposed to animated graphics, is more readily accepted by drivers (Smith et al., 2021). This aids drivers in perceiving danger, subsequently resulting in better outcomes for the DSI in the subsequent action phase, facilitating smoother and more effortless vehicle control.
Most of the eye-tracking data from our four interface designs did not yield significant results. This could be due to the quick redirection of participants’ attention to the traffic participants displayed on the interface, and the simplicity and comprehensibility of the design elements in all four designs, which did not require drivers to allocate significant cognitive processing capacity to understand any complex or obscure information. It is possible that the task difficulty in this scenario was not high enough to cause significant differences in drivers’ allocation of attentional resources across the four AR-HUD (WSD) interfaces. This calls for more precise and effective methods of measuring attention or adjustments to the urgency level of the scenario to make the changes in attentional demands more easily measurable.

7. Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, in terms of display medium, we did not compare the differences in drivers’ responses to hazardous situations between the presence and absence of AR-HUD (WSD). Second, in terms of interface design, our designs were tailored specifically to the traffic rules and scenarios in China, without considering potential variations in traffic rules and scenarios in other countries and regions.
In addition, we did not thoroughly explore the effects of different expression modes in conveying AR-HUD (WSD) information on drivers’ handling of hazards. Among the four interface designs used in our experiment, only world-fixed and world-animated presentations were investigated, and other expression approaches were not explored. Additionally, despite an a priori power analysis suggesting a sample size of 20 participants, our sample size was still relatively small. Moreover, we could not control for the potential influence of different drivers’ driving styles on their driving behavior when faced with hazards. Furthermore, we could not ensure that each participant had the same level of familiarity with our interface designs, making it difficult to draw clear conclusions about the impact of increasing familiarity with the interface designs on driving behavior. And the use of driving simulators and virtual driving scenarios may not fully reflect the extent to which our AR-HUD (WSD) interfaces would elicit similar responses and behaviors in the real world.
In terms of dependent variable measurement, we lacked more precise measures and analysis methods for participants’ attention allocation, and the complexity and difficulty of the experimental scenarios may have influenced attention allocation and workload, resulting in limited significant findings in the eye-tracking data. Furthermore, it should be noted that the variety and intricacy of the hazardous scenarios incorporated in this study were somewhat constrained. Prior research has already indicated that the complexity of driving tasks can significantly influence driving performance when using HUDs (Smith et al., 2016). Factors such as the speed, direction, and number of approaching hazards, as well as the presence of different types of traffic participants (e.g., bicycles, pedestrians), may influence drivers’ decision-making and actions when dealing with hazardous situations.
In addition to the aforementioned limitations, our proposed DSID framework also had certain constraints. Specifically, our framework only guided designers on how to design the dynamic effects of visual information but did not provide design recommendations regarding human-factors aspects, such as the color, opacity, and layout of elements. Exploring and researching these aspects will be a key focus in future work.

8. Conclusion and future work

This study investigated the impacts of AR-HUD interfaces on drivers’ SA and driving performance, based on the SRK taxonomy and SA theory. In terms of theoretical contributions, we proposed a DSID framework to guide the design of AR-HUD interfaces. In our experiments, the decision time (reaction time) of drivers using HMI2 (DSI, LW) was shorter than that of drivers using our other three schemes. Moreover, drivers’ driving behaviors were gentler when using HMI2 (DSI, LW), as evidenced by the acceleration being closer to the safe threshold and the deceleration being smaller. At the same time, HMI2 (DSI, LW) reduced the cognitive workload of drivers in responding to hazards, improving their user experience, as reflected in the higher average scores on the subjective scales corresponding to the use of HMI2 (DSI, LW). In addition, the statistical analyses of eye-tracking data showed that the higher average fixation duration, number of fixations, and visit duration of drivers on the side AOI using HMI2 (DSI, LW) indicated to some extent that HMI2 (DSI, LW) better directed drivers’ attention to lateral hazards.
The HMI2 (DSI, LW) interface displays symbol-type side warnings, sign-type speedometers, and signal-type dynamic driving space information. Compared with other schemes, using these three types of information in HMI2 (DSI, LW) provided appropriate support for drivers’ behaviors at all three levels of the SRK taxonomy in dangerous scenarios. These results also support our conclusion that DSID has the potential to help enhance driver SA in hazardous situations and improve driving safety.
In terms of practical implications, we believe that the DSID framework proposed in this study can be generalized to AR-HUD interface design in many traffic scenarios. For example, in other complex scenarios, such as left turns at intersections, AR-HUD interfaces with DSI can facilitate drivers using appropriate skill-based behaviors to deal with the actions of other traffic participants. Moreover, such interface design would not only be effective under manual driving conditions, but also at higher levels of automated driving where human and intelligent systems interact and the SA needs of the human–vehicle team change. In addition to further theoretical and methodological optimization studies, comparative studies on different dimensions of the interface need to be explored. For example, the effects of the number of colors and the animation of the color changes on the driver’s cognition and driving behavior can be investigated. It is also worth exploring the effects of different interface information layouts or representations on drivers in more complex hazardous scenarios. These issues need to be further explored in the future, and the SRK taxonomy and SA theory will continue to apply to HMI design.
